body.objective: Students will be able to use the four critique steps.
body.iCan: I can use the four critique steps.
successCriteria: I can describe what I see in an artwork
I can analyze how the elements of art are used
I can interpret meaning and judge an artwork with reasons
body.hook: Two people can look at the same painting and see completely different things. One sees a calm forest; another sees something lonely and dark. Neither is wrong, but the best art critics back up what they see with evidence. Today you'll learn a four-step method that turns "I like it" into a real response.

vocabulary.definition: To list what you see in an artwork without giving opinions.
To explain how the artist used the elements and principles of art.
To explain what you think the artwork means or expresses.
To give a reasoned opinion about an artwork's success.
The building blocks of art: line, shape, form, space, texture, value and colour.
A careful, structured response to an artwork.

study.title: The Four-Step Critique
study.question: How do I respond to art with evidence?
study.passage:
Step 1, Describe: What do you see? List subjects, colours, lines, shapes and materials. No opinions yet.
Step 2, Analyze: How is it organized? Where does your eye go first? Which elements stand out? How are balance, contrast and emphasis used?
Step 3, Interpret: What mood or idea does it express? What might the artist be saying? Use evidence: "The dark blues and heavy shapes make it feel..."
Step 4, Judge: Is it successful? Why? Judge by what the artist was trying to do, not only whether you like it.
Artworks to discuss (show images from a gallery website):
A. Emily Carr, a painting of a British Columbia forest (1930s): swirling greens, tall trunks, rhythmic brushstrokes.
B. Kenojuak Ashevak, The Enchanted Owl (1960): an Inuit print of an owl with feathers spreading in bold, flat shapes of red and black.
C. Alex Janvier, an artist from Cold Lake First Nations in Alberta: flowing, colourful lines and symbols connected to the land and Dene culture.
In groups, choose one artwork and complete all four steps on a critique sheet. Each group shares its interpretation and the evidence behind it.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; teachers show images from public gallery and museum websites.

study.product: Write a four-paragraph critique of one artwork (one paragraph per step), using at least four art vocabulary words and specific evidence.

examples.title: Describe vs interpret
examples.problem: Is "The owl looks proud" a description or an interpretation?
steps: It is an idea about meaning, not just what is seen

examples.title: Analyzing
examples.problem: How might an artist lead your eye to the main subject?
examples.answer: With strong contrast, a central placement or lines pointing toward it

examples.title: Using evidence
examples.answer: "...it uses soft greens and gentle, curving lines."
examples.explore: What evidence would show tension instead?

examples.title: Judging fairly
examples.problem: Why judge by what the artist was trying to do?
examples.answer: A bold print and a detailed painting succeed in different ways
